transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-23
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE); Jenny Cho (Redwood SE); Maya Thompson (AtlasPay - CTO); Liam O'Neil (Lead ML Eng); Priya Singh (SRE)

[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining today, hope folks can hear me okay, we have the Jenny and I to go through the latest benchmark numbers versus the baseline provider, and then align on next steps.
[00:15] Maya (AtlasPay): yes hi, loud and clear. quick update from our side we ramped a small batch of traffic last night to mirror peak, so the numbers should be a bit more realistic.
[00:30] Jenny (Redwood SE): great; quick note on agenda — i'll show median, p95 and p99 for latency, qps throughput under sustained load, and a cost-per-token comparison. some of the auto charts are in the spreadsheet Samir shared.
[00:45] Liam (AtlasPay): i took a peek — nice. one ask: can we see the raw logs for the 99th runs? the p99 looked close but i want to see distribution.
[01:05] Samir: absolutely we'll include logs. ok jenny, kick it off.

[01:20] Jenny: starting with the median latency, under our recommended profile (int8 quant, batching=8, kv-cache enabled) redwood median was 42ms per token, baseline provider was 65ms. throughput at concurrency 50 was 280 qps for Redwood and about 160 qps for baseline. those are sustained numbers with warmed cache.
[01:45] Priya: when you say warmed cache, how long was the warm period? we saw differences if cache cold.
[02:00] Jenny: good point — we warmed prefixes for 10 minutes, which matches the workload you sent (many repeated system prompts). cold start median is obviously higher — about +40% across both.
[02:15] Samir: note that the baseline did better on single-request cold scenarios for some model sizes; they have a lower single-thread overhead in their hosted endpoints, probably due to their different scheduler. but the long-tail p99 was where baseline had issues under sustained high concurrency.

[02:40] Maya: can you repeat the p95/p99 numbers? last week's summary had slightly different.
[02:55] Jenny: sure — p95 for Redwood was 210ms, p99 430ms. baseline was p95 240ms, p99 520ms. but there's nuance: for some payloads with long context length (context>2k tokens) baseline p99 shot to 800ms, while Redwood stayed around 510ms due to our kv-cache and chunking.
[03:20] Liam: is kv-cache the same as KV cache? i saw a note in the spreadsheet that said 'KV cash' — small typo.
[03:30] Jenny: yeah, sorry transcription/typo in sheet, that's KV-cache.
[03:35] Priya: any quality delta with int8 quant? we got occasional hallucination or answer truncation last test.
[03:50] Jenny: we ran quantization A/B — int8 gives the best perf/cost tradeoff with minimal regression on your eval set (WER and factuality checks). there were a few edge-case regressions on long arithmetic sequences, we flagged those in the evals doc. if quality is critical we can run int8-quant + dynamic fallback to fp16 for flagged prompts.
[04:15] Samir: operationally that's easy — route based on prompt tags or call a fallback path for heavy-prompts.

[04:30] Maya: cost model — you mentioned per-token costs. how do the numbers look for us at our projected 10m tokens / month?
[04:50] Samir: using the benchmarked throughput + batching profile, Redwood estimate is approx $X per million tokens; baseline is ~20-30% higher given their less efficient batching/caching. we'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet — it's in the next steps.
[05:05] Liam: what's the impact of Dedicated vs Hosted here — are these numbers on hosted shared infra?
[05:20] Jenny: these benchmark runs were on Redwood hosted POC infra with reserved concurrency to mimic dedicated behavior. Dedicated pools will reduce jitter and tail latency further; we can provision a small dedicated pool for your pilot to test real dedicated numbers.
[05:35] Priya: security wise, does the dedicated option still give us audit logs + KMS?
[05:45] Samir: yes — Dedicated + Private options both integrate with your KMS and provide audit logs and VPC peering. we can share SOC2/ISO docs after the call.

[06:00] Maya: okay back to perf — you mentioned baseline had a scheduler that helps cold single-requests. can you explain why Redwood is better at sustained throughput?
[06:20] Jenny: sure — two reasons: one, our runtime does continuous batching and fine-grained kernel selection optimized for batched generation, plus our KV-cache implementation avoids re-computing history when prompts share prefixes. two, our quantization-friendly kernels reduce per-token compute. the baseline provider optimized their single-call latency but at scale their scheduler doesn't batch as aggressively, so they lose efficiency under sustained qps.
[06:50] Liam: can you quantify the batching effect? like how much of the latency reduction is due to batching vs quantization?
[07:05] Jenny: rough split from experiments: ~40-50% of throughput gain came from batching at concurrency 50; quantization contributed ~25-35% lower per-token time; cache contributed another 15-20% depending on prompt reuse. these are approximate.

[07:30] (short crosstalk)
[07:40] Priya: any memory overhead concerns with kv-cache for long contexts? we don't want OOMs on heavy users.
[07:55] Jenny: we have LRU sharding and per-session KV eviction; for extremely long contexts we recommend using chunking with on-disk checkpointing on Dedicated if needed. we'll share configuration suggestions in the doc.

[08:20] Samir: quick note on the p99 tests — we saw some spikes around 520ms that correlate with garbage collection on the host VM; we think dedicated GPU pools reduce that variance.
[08:35] Maya: is that something the baseline also suffers from?
[08:45] Jenny: yes, but their spikes were higher under the same load. we also noticed alternative network tail latency at certain times which we'll annotate in the logs.

[09:00] Liam: audio is fine, thanks. can we try a run with batching=4 and batching=16 to see sensitivity?
[09:15] Jenny: yes, we have those runs queued. quick preview — batching=4 reduces median latency but lowers throughput; batching=16 improves throughput but slightly increases median due to queueing delay. the sweet spot depends on your SLOs.
[09:35] Maya: regarding SLOs, we want 95% < 300ms and 99% < 500ms for most user-facing flows. can we hit that?
[09:50] Jenny: in our recommended profile we hit p95 ~210ms and p99 ~430ms, so yes for most flows we're within target. we need to validate on representative prompts with the warm cache; cold starts will be higher.
[10:10] Samir: operational next step — we'll run a targeted 99th percentile long-run (6-8 hours) with mixed prompt set and share full logs and annotated spreadsheet.

[10:30] Maya: on the quality front, we'd like to see the flagged prompts where int8 regressed. can you add that to the doc?
[10:40] Jenny: yep, i'll add a small eval table and examples.

[10:55] Priya: also will you include the billing estimate for Dedicated pilot vs hosted? we need to sign off.
[11:05] Samir: yes, Samir answer: I'll include committed capacity pricing and a short model of per-hour cost for a 3-node dedicated pool.

[11:20] (Background typing)
[11:30] Liam: one more — do you support canary rollouts / A/B with automatic fallback if latency exceeds threshold? we want to ramp and fallback automatically.
[11:45] Jenny: yes, Redwood Console supports canary/A-B and automated fallback policies; we can demo that in the deep-dive.

[12:00] Maya: good. final ask — share SOC2 docs and network diagram.
[12:10] Samir: will do after call.

[12:25] Recap / Next steps:
Samir: we'll share updated benchmark CSV + cost model by 2025-07-25.
Jenny: i'll run the 99th percentile long-run and the batching sensitivity tests and post logs by 2025-07-29.
Liam: we'll provide the final prompt set and traffic mix by 2025-07-28.

[12:50] Maya: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[13:00] Samir: thanks all, see you next week.
[13:10] (call ends)
